curriculum.title: Abraham and Blessing for the Nations

core.big_idea: God's promises to Abraham move the biblical story toward blessing for all nations.

passages.reading_note: Identify command, promises, and worldwide purpose.
Observe promise, doubt, reassurance, and belief.
Use in extension to examine Paul’s later canonical interpretation.

core.metanarrative_position: Promise and covenant: one family becomes the chosen path toward blessing for all nations and ultimately Christ.
core.biblical_genre: Patriarchal narrative with covenant promise; epistle for later canonical comparison

claims.statement: God commands Abram to go and promises land, nationhood, a great name, blessing, and worldwide purpose.
Abram travels through the land and builds altars to the Lord.
Genesis 15 portrays Abram voicing uncertainty, God renewing the promise, and Abram believing the Lord.
The Abrahamic promise is not merely private prosperity; its stated purpose includes all families of the earth.
claims.interpretive_hinge: The repeated blessing language culminates in a worldwide purpose.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not reduce blessing to wealth or promise every believer Abraham’s exact land and descendant terms.

claims.statement: Paul later connects the promise to the gospel among the nations and to Christ.

core.interpretation_skill: Map promise terms, compare immediate Genesis meaning with later canonical interpretation, and avoid prosperity assumptions.

learning.foundation_objective: Explain the principal promises to Abraham and locate them on the whole-Bible timeline.
learning.extension_objective: Compare Genesis and Galatians, distinguishing the original promise wording from Paul’s later canonical interpretation.
know: Genesis 12 includes land, family, name, blessing, and nations.
Genesis 15 includes Abram’s question and faith.
Galatians links the promise to gospel blessing and Christ.
understand: God’s election of one family serves a wider mission.
Faith is trust in God’s promise, not denial of unanswered questions.
practise: Use a gift or opportunity to bless someone outside the usual friendship circle.
Bring honest questions to God rather than pretending certainty.
become: A student who understands chosen blessing as service for the good of others.
success_evidence: The student completes the promise map accurately.
The student explains why prosperity language is inadequate.
The student distinguishes Genesis wording from Galatians interpretation.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students map God’s promises to Abraham and explain their worldwide purpose.
zero_prep_card.opening: Ask: Can someone be chosen for a task that is meant to help many others? Give a non-competitive example.
say: God calls Abram and gives several connected promises.
The repeated blessing language ends with all families of the earth.
Abram asks an honest question in Genesis 15, and God renews the promise.
Later, Galatians connects this promise with the gospel and Christ.
ask: What does God command Abram to do?
What promise categories can you list?
Who is included in the purpose of blessing?
How does Genesis 15 portray faith and questions together?
zero_prep_card.do: Complete the Abraham Promise Map and add the outward arrow toward all nations.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for trusting faith and for blessings to become service rather than self-centred privilege.

preparation.passage_context: Genesis 12 opens the Abraham cycle after Babel. The narrative narrows to one family but explicitly gives that family a worldwide purpose. Genesis 15 develops the descendant promise and Abram’s faith.
text_observations: Genesis 12:1 contains a command; verses 2-3 contain a sequence of promises.
“Bless” appears repeatedly and culminates in all families of the earth.
Genesis 15 includes uncertainty, divine reassurance, and credited faith.
interpretation_notes: Define covenant progressively; Genesis 15 contains a formal covenant scene beyond the selected opening verses.
Use Galatians as a later inspired interpretation, not as though Abram already possessed Paul’s full vocabulary.
Distinguish blessing from comfort, wealth, status, or national superiority.
theological_guardrails: Do not teach ethnic or spiritual superiority as the meaning of election.
Do not make honest questions the opposite of faith.
Do not force every Old Testament “seed” reference into a simplistic prediction without context.

likely_questions.question: Why did God choose Abraham?
likely_questions.purpose: The text gives the purpose of worldwide blessing but not an exhaustive reason for choosing this individual; avoid speculation.

likely_questions.question: Does faith mean Abraham never doubted?
likely_questions.purpose: Genesis records questions and later failures; faith can bring uncertainty to God and continue trusting.

discussion_questions.question: What are the promise categories in Genesis 12:1-3?
Why does “all families of the earth” matter?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain election for service rather than superiority.

discussion_questions.question: What does Abram’s question in Genesis 15 show?
What does Galatians add to our reading?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Distinguish later interpretation from original narrative awareness.

activities.title: Abraham Promise Map
steps: Add Land, Descendants, Name, and Blessing.
Draw the outward arrow to All Families.
Add Galatians in a different colour as later interpretation.
activities.learning_link: Visualises both the promise structure and canonical development.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Draw the map on the board.

activities.title: Chosen for Service Cases
steps: Rewrite a self-centred use as service.

closing.prayer_prompt: Ask for faith that brings honest questions and uses blessings for others.
closing.take_home_line: God chose Abraham’s family so blessing would reach all nations.

family.title: Blessed for a Wider Purpose
family.parent_intro: This study maps the promises to Abraham and asks how chosen blessing serves others.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Read Genesis 12:1-3 and 15:1-6; older students may add Galatians 3:8.
List the promises and circle “all families of the earth.”
Draw a centre circle for Abraham and arrows toward Land, Family, Blessing, and All Nations.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: How can faith include an honest question?
How can something good our family has become good for others?

interactive.title: Promise Map
interactive.instructions: Create a visual map of the promise and its worldwide purpose.

family.weekly_action: Choose one outward-facing act of hospitality, generosity, or encouragement.
family.prayer: God, thank You for Your promises. Teach us to trust You and use what we receive for the good of others.
family.parent_note: Avoid prosperity claims and comparisons that present one ethnic group or congregation as inherently superior.

quiz.question: Which phrase gives the promise a worldwide purpose?
Genesis 15 shows Abram asking an honest question.
quiz.explanation: Abram voices his concern before God renews the promise.

quiz.question: What does Galatians connect to the promise?
options: The gospel among the nations and Christ

answer.text: The gospel among the nations and Christ

quiz.explanation: Paul provides a later canonical synthesis.

quiz.question: Which reading should be rejected?
quiz.explanation: The promise cannot be reduced to prosperity.

puzzle.title: Promise Category Match
puzzle.instructions: Match each phrase to its category.
items: Go to the land I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation.
In you all families shall be blessed.

pairs.prompt: Go to the land I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation.
In you all families shall be blessed.

printables.title: Abraham Promise Map
printables.purpose: Map the Genesis promise categories and distinguish later canonical interpretation.

accessibility.reading_level: Upper-primary discussion with concrete anchors before abstract explanation.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Define covenant, genre, inference, and other technical terms before expecting use.
neurodiversity_supports: Use a visible timeline or comparison grid.
Allow written, drawn, or spoken responses.
Model one completed example before independent work.
sensory_notes: Offer a seated alternative to movement activities.
non_reader_support: Use prepared cards so participation does not depend on fluent reading.

do_not_ask: Do not rank families, ethnic groups, or congregations as more valuable.
Do not ask students to disclose family infertility, adoption, or migration stories.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Keep personal examples optional and frame election as responsibility for blessing, not superiority.
